title: RBI Restores 90% Daily CRR Floor From December 1, Reversing October Tightening
excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India has cut the minimum daily cash reserve maintenance requirement from 99% to 90% of the prescribed CRR, effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026, as banking-system liquidity swings from surplus to deficit. The CRR rate itself stays at 3%.
body:
• The RBI has reduced the minimum daily maintenance of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% of the requirement to 90%, effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026.
  • The prescribed CRR rate itself is unchanged at 3% of banks' deposits; only the daily floor within each fortnight has moved.
  • The decision reverses the October 2026 tightening in full, restoring the position that held before October 16, after system liquidity swung from surplus to deficit over the last four months.
  • For readers: no action is needed on deposits or loans. Treasury heads quoted by BusinessLine say the relief is operational flexibility, not fresh liquidity.

The Reserve Bank of India on Friday, November 27, cut the minimum daily cash reserve maintenance requirement for scheduled banks from 99 per cent of the prescribed requirement to 90 per cent, effective from the reporting fortnight beginning December 1, 2026. The decision, issued under Section 42(1) of the RBI Act, 1934 through circular RBI/2026-27/310, restores the status quo that held until mid-October.

In its notification, the central bank said the change followed "an assessment of the current and evolving macroeconomic situation and liquidity conditions." The circular, signed by Chief General Manager-in-Charge J P Sharma, applies to all scheduled banks.

What the number counts

The CRR is the slice of a bank's deposits that must be parked with the RBI; the ratio currently stands at 3 per cent, and balances held as CRR earn no interest. Banks must meet that requirement on average across each reporting fortnight, but a daily floor governs how low the balance can fall on any single day. Counted here: the minimum share of the prescribed CRR that must be in place every day — 90% from December 1, down from 99%. Not counted: the CRR rate itself, which has not changed, and the fortnightly average, which banks must still meet in full.

Why the October tightening happened, and why it is being undone

The RBI had raised the daily floor from 90 per cent to 99 per cent from the fortnight beginning October 16, 2026. According to BusinessLine, that step was taken because variable rate reverse repo auctions were not proving sufficient to absorb the surplus rupee liquidity generated by the US dollar–rupee forex swap facility the RBI offered for fresh FCNR (B) deposits mobilised by banks between June 8 and August 31, 2026. With liquidity swinging from surplus to deficit over the last four months, the tighter daily floor had become a compliance strain, and the central bank has now unwound it within two months.

"The RBI's decision to restore the minimum daily CRR requirement to 90 per cent from 99 per cent, effective December 1, is a welcome relief for banks. It eases the tightrope in day-to-day CRR management, provides greater operational flexibility and helps moderate liquidity pressures."

— V Rama Chandra Reddy, Head of Treasury, Karur Vysya Bank, quoted in BusinessLine

Reddy noted that banks had continued to hold substantial balances in the Standing Deposit Facility even under the tighter regime, reflecting uneven distribution of liquidity across the system, and said the change could lower those balances as banks manage CRR more efficiently. K Arvind, Head of Treasury at Tamilnad Mercantile Bank, told BusinessLine the move "provides some operational flexibility in maintaining daily CRR," adding that banks had been keeping excess CRR to avoid any slip-up in complying with the statutory ratio.

What it does not do

Both treasury heads were clear on the limit of the measure: it injects no additional liquidity into the banking system. No new funds are released, deposit and lending rates do not change by virtue of this circular, and banks must still hold the full prescribed CRR across each fortnight. What changes is the day-to-day room banks have to let balances dip toward the floor on heavy outflow days and rebuild them later in the fortnight.

What to watch

The new floor applies from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026; until then the 99% requirement remains in force. The next test of the RBI's liquidity stance will be system liquidity readings through December and any further operations the central bank announces alongside its regular policy communications.
